question: What is a linear combination of vectors v1, ..., vp?
reference: A linear combination of v1, ..., vp is a vector y = c1 v1 + ... + cp vp, where the scalars c1, ..., cp are called the weights.

question: What is the span of vectors v1, ..., vp in R^n?
reference: Span{v1, ..., vp} is the set of all linear combinations of v1, ..., vp, i.e. all vectors that can be written as c1 v1 + ... + cp vp with scalars c1, ..., cp. It is a subset of R^n.

question: When is an indexed set of vectors {v1, ..., vp} linearly independent?
reference: The set is linearly independent if the vector equation x1 v1 + ... + xp vp = 0 has only the trivial solution. It is linearly dependent if there are weights, not all zero, that satisfy the equation (a linear dependence relation).

question: What are a pivot position and a pivot column of a matrix?
reference: A pivot position in a matrix A is a location that corresponds to a leading 1 in the reduced echelon form of A. A pivot column is a column of A that contains a pivot position.

question: What is a linear transformation?
reference: A transformation T is linear if T(u + v) = T(u) + T(v) for all u, v in its domain and T(cu) = cT(u) for all u and all scalars c. Consequently T(0) = 0 and T preserves linear combinations.

question: What does it mean for a mapping T: R^n -> R^m to be one-to-one, and to be onto R^m?
reference: T is one-to-one if each b in R^m is the image of at most one x in R^n. T is onto R^m if each b in R^m is the image of at least one x in R^n, i.e. the range of T is all of R^m.

question: What is an invertible matrix?
reference: An n x n matrix A is invertible if there is an n x n matrix C such that CA = I and AC = I, where I is the n x n identity matrix. C is uniquely determined and is called the inverse of A, written A^-1. A matrix that is not invertible is called singular.

question: What is an elementary matrix?
reference: An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained by performing a single elementary row operation (replacement, interchange or scaling) on an identity matrix. Every elementary matrix is invertible; its inverse is the elementary matrix of the same type that transforms it back into I.

question: What is the null space of a matrix?
reference: The null space Nul A of an m x n matrix A is the set of all solutions of the homogeneous equation Ax = 0. It is a subspace of R^n.

question: What is a basis for a subspace?
reference: A basis for a subspace H is a linearly independent set in H that spans H.

question: How is the determinant of an n x n matrix defined?
reference: For n >= 2, the determinant of an n x n matrix A is the sum of n terms of the form a1j det A1j with alternating plus and minus signs, where A1j is the submatrix obtained by deleting row 1 and column j of A (cofactor expansion across the first row). The determinant can be computed by a cofactor expansion across any row or down any column.

question: What is a vector space?
reference: A vector space is a nonempty set V of objects called vectors, on which two operations, addition and multiplication by scalars, are defined and satisfy ten axioms: closure under addition and scalar multiplication, commutativity and associativity of addition, existence of a zero vector and of additive inverses, the two distributive laws, (cd)u = c(du), and 1u = u.

question: What is the rank of a matrix?
reference: The rank of A is the dimension of the column space of A. It equals the number of pivot columns (pivot positions) of A and also the dimension of the row space of A.

question: What are an eigenvector and an eigenvalue of a square matrix?
reference: An eigenvector of an n x n matrix A is a nonzero vector x such that Ax = lambda x for some scalar lambda. A scalar lambda is an eigenvalue of A if Ax = lambda x has a nontrivial solution x; such an x is an eigenvector corresponding to lambda.

question: When is a square matrix diagonalizable?
reference: A square matrix A is diagonalizable if it is similar to a diagonal matrix, i.e. A = PDP^-1 for some invertible matrix P and diagonal matrix D. By the Diagonalization Theorem, an n x n matrix is diagonalizable if and only if it has n linearly independent eigenvectors.

question: How are the matrix equation Ax = b, the vector equation x1 a1 + ... + xn an = b and the linear system with augmented matrix [a1 ... an b] related?
reference: They have the same solution set (Theorem 3 in Section 1.4). In particular, Ax = b has a solution if and only if b is a linear combination of the columns of A.

question: How is the solution set of a consistent equation Ax = b related to the solution set of the homogeneous equation Ax = 0?
reference: If p is any particular solution of Ax = b, then the solution set of Ax = b is the set of all vectors w = p + vh, where vh is any solution of Ax = 0. Geometrically, it is the solution set of Ax = 0 translated by p.

question: How is the linear independence of the columns of a matrix A related to the equation Ax = 0?
reference: The columns of A are linearly independent if and only if Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution. Each linear dependence relation among the columns corresponds to a nontrivial solution of Ax = 0.

question: How is a linear transformation T: R^n -> R^m related to its standard matrix?
reference: There is a unique m x n matrix A such that T(x) = Ax for all x in R^n. Its j-th column is T(ej), the image of the j-th column of the n x n identity matrix: A = [T(e1) ... T(en)]. A is called the standard matrix of T.

question: How are the properties one-to-one and onto of a linear transformation related to its standard matrix?
reference: For a linear transformation T: R^n -> R^m with standard matrix A: T maps R^n onto R^m if and only if the columns of A span R^m; T is one-to-one if and only if the columns of A are linearly independent, which is equivalent to T(x) = 0 having only the trivial solution.

question: How are elementary row operations related to elementary matrices?
reference: If an elementary row operation is performed on an m x n matrix A, the result can be written as EA, where the m x m matrix E is obtained by performing the same row operation on I_m. Each elementary matrix is invertible, and its inverse is the elementary matrix of the reverse operation.

question: How can row reduction be used to find the inverse of a matrix?
reference: An n x n matrix A is invertible if and only if it is row equivalent to I_n, and any sequence of elementary row operations that reduces A to I_n also transforms I_n into A^-1 (Theorem 7 in Section 2.2). Algorithm: row reduce the augmented matrix [A I]; if A is row equivalent to I, then [A I] is row equivalent to [I A^-1]; otherwise A has no inverse.

question: How do elementary row operations affect the determinant of a square matrix?
reference: Adding a multiple of one row to another row does not change the determinant; interchanging two rows changes its sign; multiplying one row by k multiplies the determinant by k.

question: How is the determinant of a product AB related to the determinants of A and B, and how is det A^T related to det A?
reference: For n x n matrices, det AB = (det A)(det B) (multiplicative property), and det A^T = det A.

question: What is the geometric meaning of the determinant of a 2 x 2 or 3 x 3 matrix?
reference: For a 2 x 2 matrix A, |det A| is the area of the parallelogram determined by the columns of A; for a 3 x 3 matrix, |det A| is the volume of the parallelepiped determined by its columns. A linear transformation x -> Ax multiplies areas (volumes) of regions by |det A|.

question: How are the kernel and the range of a linear transformation related to the null space and the column space of a matrix?
reference: The kernel of a linear transformation T: V -> W is the set of all u in V with T(u) = 0, and the range is the set of all vectors T(x) in W. If T(x) = Ax for a matrix A, the kernel and the range of T are exactly Nul A and Col A. The kernel is a subspace of V and the range is a subspace of W.

question: How are the rank of an m x n matrix A and the dimension of its null space related?
reference: By the Rank Theorem, rank A + dim Nul A = n, the number of columns of A. The rank equals the number of pivot positions and dim Nul A equals the number of free variables in Ax = 0.

question: How are the pivot columns of a matrix related to its column space?
reference: The pivot columns of A form a basis for Col A. The pivot columns of A itself must be used, not those of its echelon form, because row operations can change the column space.

question: How are eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues related to linear independence?
reference: If v1, ..., vr are eigenvectors corresponding to distinct eigenvalues lambda1, ..., lambdar of an n x n matrix, then {v1, ..., vr} is linearly independent. As a consequence, an n x n matrix with n distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable.

question: How are similar matrices related in terms of their characteristic polynomials and eigenvalues?
reference: A is similar to B if there is an invertible matrix P such that P^-1 A P = B. Similar matrices have the same characteristic polynomial and hence the same eigenvalues with the same multiplicities.

question: Which concepts must be understood before studying the concept of a basis?
reference: A basis is defined as a linearly independent set in a subspace H that spans H, so the prerequisites are subspace, linear independence and span (and, through span, linear combination).

question: Which concepts must be understood before studying the dimension of a subspace or vector space?
reference: Dimension is the number of vectors in any basis, so it requires the concept of a basis (and with it subspace, linear independence and span), together with the fact that all bases of a space have the same number of vectors.

question: Which concepts must be understood before studying eigenvectors and eigenvalues?
reference: The definition Ax = lambda x with x nonzero for an n x n matrix A requires square matrices, the matrix-vector product Ax, scalar multiples of vectors, and the notion of a nonzero (nontrivial) solution.

question: Which concepts must be understood before studying diagonalizable matrices?
reference: A diagonalizable matrix is similar to a diagonal matrix (A = PDP^-1), so it requires diagonal matrices, similar matrices and invertible matrices; the Diagonalization Theorem additionally uses eigenvectors and linear independence.

question: Which concepts must be understood before studying the rank of a matrix?
reference: Rank is the dimension of the column space, so it requires the column space and dimension (and therefore basis); computing it uses pivot columns.

question: Which concepts must be understood before studying the eigenspace of a matrix?
reference: The eigenspace of A corresponding to lambda is the null space of A - lambda I, so it requires eigenvalues (and eigenvectors) and the null space of a matrix (and subspaces).

question: Which concepts must be understood before studying the characteristic equation of a matrix?
reference: The characteristic equation is det(A - lambda I) = 0, so it requires determinants, eigenvalues and the identity matrix; it relies on the fact that A - lambda I is not invertible exactly when det(A - lambda I) = 0.

question: Which concepts must be understood before studying the change-of-coordinates matrix between two bases?
reference: The columns of the change-of-coordinates matrix P(C<-B) are the C-coordinate vectors of the vectors in basis B, and [x]C = P(C<-B)[x]B, so it requires bases and coordinate vectors relative to a basis.

question: Which concepts must be understood before studying the LU factorization?
reference: In A = LU, L is a unit lower triangular matrix and U is an echelon form of A obtained by row reduction (without row interchanges), so it requires echelon forms, lower triangular matrices and row reduction.

question: Which concepts must be understood before studying invertible matrices?
reference: An invertible matrix A satisfies CA = I and AC = I for some n x n matrix C, so it requires square matrices, the identity matrix and matrix multiplication.

question: Which conditions are equivalent to the invertibility of an n x n matrix A? List the conditions that the textbook adds to the Invertible Matrix Theorem in later chapters as well.
reference: Section 2.3: A is row equivalent to I_n; A has n pivot positions; Ax = 0 has only the trivial solution; the columns of A are linearly independent; x -> Ax is one-to-one; Ax = b has at least one solution for each b; the columns of A span R^n; x -> Ax maps R^n onto R^n; there are matrices C and D with CA = I and AD = I; A^T is invertible. Sections 2.9 and 4.6: the columns of A form a basis of R^n; Col A = R^n; dim Col A = n; rank A = n; Nul A = {0}; dim Nul A = 0. Section 3.2: det A is not zero. Section 5.2: the number 0 is not an eigenvalue of A.

question: How can the determinant be used to decide whether the columns of a square matrix are linearly independent?
reference: For a square matrix A, the columns are linearly independent if and only if A is invertible (Invertible Matrix Theorem), and A is invertible if and only if det A is not zero. Hence the columns are linearly independent exactly when det A is nonzero; det A = 0 when the columns (or rows) are linearly dependent.

question: How are determinants used to find the eigenvalues of a matrix, and how are the corresponding eigenvectors then found?
reference: lambda is an eigenvalue of A if and only if (A - lambda I)x = 0 has a nontrivial solution, i.e. A - lambda I is not invertible, i.e. det(A - lambda I) = 0. The eigenvalues are therefore the roots of the characteristic equation det(A - lambda I) = 0. The eigenvectors for lambda are the nonzero solutions of (A - lambda I)x = 0, found by row reduction; together with 0 they form the eigenspace Nul(A - lambda I).

question: How does the notion of a subspace of R^n generalize to vector spaces, and which subspaces associated with a matrix appear in both settings?
reference: A subspace of R^n is a set that contains the zero vector and is closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication (Section 2.8). In Section 4.1 a subspace of a general vector space V is defined by the same three properties. In both settings Span{v1, ..., vp} is a subspace, the null space Nul A of an m x n matrix is a subspace of R^n, and the column space Col A is a subspace of R^m.

question: How can the dimension of the null space of a matrix be determined from row reduction, and how is it related to the free variables of Ax = 0?
reference: Row reduce A and write the general solution of Ax = 0 as a linear combination of vectors whose weights are the free variables (one vector for each free variable); and these vectors form a basis for Nul A. Hence dim Nul A equals the number of free variables, while dim Col A equals the number of pivot columns. Ax = 0 has a nontrivial solution exactly when there is at least one free variable.

question: How does a basis of an n-dimensional vector space V allow V to be studied like R^n?
reference: By the Unique Representation Theorem, every x in V can be written uniquely as x = c1 b1 + ... + cn bn; the weights form the coordinate vector [x]B. The coordinate mapping x -> [x]B is a one-to-one linear transformation from V onto R^n, i.e. an isomorphism, so vector space operations and questions such as linear independence or spanning in V can be translated into the same questions about coordinate vectors in R^n.

question: How is the diagonalization A = PDP^-1 interpreted in terms of the matrix of a linear transformation relative to a basis?
reference: If A = PDP^-1 with D diagonal, and B is the basis of R^n formed by the columns of P (eigenvectors of A), then D is the B-matrix of the transformation x -> Ax (Diagonal Matrix Representation theorem). P plays the role of the change-of-coordinates matrix P_B from Section 4.4, so in B-coordinates the transformation simply scales each coordinate by an eigenvalue.

question: What does the rank of an n x n matrix A tell us about the solutions of Ax = b?
reference: If rank A = n, then A is invertible (Invertible Matrix Theorem), so for each b the equation Ax = b has the unique solution x = A^-1 b. If rank A < n, then dim Nul A = n - rank A > 0, Ax = 0 has nontrivial solutions, A is not invertible, and Ax = b fails to have a solution for some b and has infinitely many solutions whenever it is consistent.

question: How is row reduction to echelon form used to compute a determinant?
reference: Reduce A to an echelon form U using only row replacements and row interchanges. Replacements do not change the determinant and each interchange changes its sign, so det A = (-1)^r det U, where r is the number of interchanges. U is triangular, so det U is the product of its diagonal entries. Thus det A = (-1)^r times the product of the pivots in U when A is invertible, and det A = 0 when A is not invertible.

question: How does Cramer's rule connect determinants with solving linear systems and with the inverse of a matrix?
reference: For an invertible n x n matrix A and any b, the unique solution of Ax = b has entries xi = det Ai(b) / det A, where Ai(b) is A with column i replaced by b (Cramer's rule). Applying this to the columns of the identity matrix gives the inverse formula A^-1 = (1/det A) adj A, where adj A, the adjugate, is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors. These formulas are mainly of theoretical use; row reduction is more efficient for large matrices.
